Torin stood before the reception desk, his hands clasped tightly behind his back as he looked at Ekaterina with a mixture of hope and expectation. "I need your honest assessment on a plan I have for my mother’s legacy," he began, his voice steady but urgent. "I intend to donate her entire quilt collection here so I can visit them on permanent display."

Ekaterina offered a polite nod, her expression calm and professional. "Thank you for considering our institution for such a meaningful donation," she replied smoothly. "It is an honor to assist you in preserving this important family history."

Torin leaned forward slightly, resting his elbows on the counter. "My thinking is simple: if they are part of the museum’s core collection, they should be visible year-round so I can walk by and feel close to her."

Ekaterina adjusted her glasses, maintaining eye contact. "I appreciate your sentiment, but I must clarify that museums rarely maintain permanent displays for textile collections. Preservation requires rotation to protect the fibers from light exposure."

Torin frowned, pulling back from the counter. "That sounds inefficient. If I give them to you, I expect them to be showcased, not hidden away. Is that not standard practice?"

"While we showcase beautiful works," Ekaterina continued, her tone remaining even, "most donations enter our climate-controlled archives for safety. They are typically viewed only during special exhibitions or by researchers."

"That defeats the purpose entirely," Torin said, his voice tightening. "If I cannot see them regularly, what is the point of donating them versus just storing them myself?"

"Donating ensures professional conservation that prevents deterioration over decades," Ekaterina explained gently. "It preserves the integrity of the work even when it is not publicly visible."

"I disagree," Torin countered sharply. "If they are in storage, I am losing access to my mother’s memory just the same as if I threw them away."

"You would retain the knowledge that her craft is professionally safeguarded for future generations," Ekaterina said, lifting a pen to gesture toward the brochure on the desk. "We can also arrange specific viewing appointments for donors upon request."

"So there is no guarantee of visibility, and I have to schedule appointments just to look at my own heritage," Torin muttered, rubbing his temple. "This feels like a poor arrangement."

"I understand your concern, and I assure you the care provided is exceptional," Ekaterina said. "Would you like to review the donor agreement details to see how scheduling works?"

"Maybe," Torin sighed, looking down at his shoes. "But I wanted a simpler solution where I could just walk in and see them. This complication makes me hesitant."

"Please take the time needed to weigh these options carefully," Ekaterina assured him. "We are here to support whatever decision brings you peace of mind."

"Fine. Send me those documents," Torin decided, straightening up. "I will read them before making a final commitment on whether this path is right for me."

"Certainly. I will email those materials to you later today for your convenience," Ekaterina replied, offering a small smile. "Thank you again for your interest in our museum."

"Okay. I will get back to you once I have reviewed the terms thoroughly," Torin said, turning toward the exit. "Do not expect a quick answer."

"Understood. We look forward to hearing from you when you are ready to proceed," Ekaterina called softly after him.
plan: Torin believes that if he donates his mother's quilts to the museum, they will be put on permanent display so he can visit them whenever he wants to feel close to her.
flaw: Museums rarely keep donated items on permanent display; most collections are rotated, and many donated quilts end up in climate-controlled storage, seen only occasionally by curators or researchers. Torin would likely find that his mother's quilts are not visible during most visits.

The workshop air was thick with the scent of sawdust and drying glue. Selah held up a board of quartersawn oak, its medullary rays creating a distinct flecked pattern across the surface. She extended it toward Victor, who stood by the workbench, wiping his hands on a rag.

"I need your opinion on this quartersawn oak for a sliding lid," Selah said.

Victor stopped wiping his hands and looked at the wood, then at her. "Thank you for asking my advice regarding your material selection today."

Selah tapped the edge of the board with her fingernail. "My plan is to use this cut so the face stays stable across its width during humidity changes."

Victor nodded slowly, his expression remaining neutral. "That is a thoughtful consideration for dimensional stability in your design."

She stepped closer, leaning over the bench to point out the straight grain lines. "It ensures the lid slides smoothly regardless of seasonal shifts, which is why I chose it."

" I appreciate your focus on consistent performance throughout the year," Victor replied, his tone measured.

Selah raised an eyebrow, waiting for validation. "Do you agree that this specific grain orientation solves the binding issue?"

Victor folded his arms, shifting his weight slightly. "I must clarify that sliding movement occurs along the grain direction."

"But the expansion happens across the width, so this cut prevents that interference," Selah countered, her voice sharpening slightly.

"All wood expands minimally along the grain, so the cut does not affect slide length," Victor stated, keeping his eyes on hers.

Selah frowned, processing the technical correction. "So you are saying my analysis of the width stability is irrelevant here?"

"The binding is governed by the box opening width, not the lid face orientation," Victor explained calmly.

Selah lowered the board, resting it back on the table. The tension in her shoulders eased as she absorbed the logic. "Then quartersawn stock provides no advantage for the sliding mechanism itself."

"You are correct; standard flat-sawn wood performs equally well for the lid," Victor confirmed.

Selah let out a short breath, running a hand through her hair. "I suppose I was overcomplicating the mechanics of the seasonal fit."

"Simplifying your approach will save time while achieving the desired result," Victor said, picking up his chisel again.
plan: Selah plans to choose quartersawn oak for the sliding lid so that the flat-sawn face of the lid will stay dimensionally stable across its width and slide smoothly regardless of seasonal humidity changes.
flaw: Quartersawn lumber is stable across its width, but a sliding lid's critical movement is along the grain direction (length), where all wood species expand and contract very little anyway; the lid's fit is governed by the cross-grain width of the box opening, not the lid's face orientation, so choosing quartersawn stock for the lid does not solve the seasonal binding Selah is worried about.
